transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-03
Time: 08:00 AM PST / 15:00 UTC
Duration: 43 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Maya Torres (Borealis Head of Platform), Liam O'Donnell (CTO), Rashida Khan (SRE), Evan Wu (FinOps)

Summary: Quick console walkthrough focused on route-level telemetry, how to map costs back to product features, and options for lowering per-token/unit economics. Went through a sample playbook and agreed on benchmarks + security follow-up.

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you making time. Quick intros then we'll jump into the console — I'm Alex, AE on the account, and Priya is our systems engineer who will run the deep bits.
[00:22] Maya Torres: Hi, Maya here, head of platform. We've got Liam on for architecture and Rashida will handle infra questions. Evan is here for the finance side.
[00:34] Liam O'Donnell: Morning. Quick ask up front — we need to see per-route cost mapping so product teams can be charged back.
[00:40] Alex Chen: Absolutely that's the core of today's demo. We'll show the usage lens, route breakdown, and the cost decomposition.
[00:53] Priya Nair: I'll also highlight configuration knobs — batching, KV cache, quant profiles — and show how those change the unit cost in the console.
[01:10] Rashida Khan: Also need to confirm our security reqs. SOC two compliance, SSO via SAML, and KMS integrations are must-haves for our legal team.
[01:20] Alex Chen: Totally, we'll touch on those and capture a follow-up to share SOC2 and deployment docs.

[01:35] Priya Nair: Ok jumping into the console — here's the landing page: top row shows total tokens, avg latency, and an estimated cost per hour based on recent traffic. Down the left is the 'Routes' tab — that's what teams use to map feature endpoints to costs.
[01:58] [screen share noise]
[02:10] Priya Nair: Clicking into Routes we get a list: chat-widget, search-embedding, doc-summarize, support-bot. Each row has usage (calls, tokens), avg latency, and a cost column that is the attributed spend. You can filter by model, time-range, customer id, or environment.
[02:40] Evan Wu: How is cost attributed? Is it token-based only?
[02:48] Priya Nair: Good question — it's decomposed. We show a token cost (model compute) plus infra overhead (GPU minutes, memory), and then any caching savings as a negative. It's not just a flat token price. We use per-route model selection and kernel profiles so your math is more precise than token-only.
[03:15] Maya Torres: Can we export per-route cost to our billing system?
[03:22] Alex Chen: Yes, CSV export and API endpoints. You can also push to S3 or connect to your internal billing pipeline.

[03:40] Priya Nair: Here's a quick drilldown on doc-summarize — you can see the distribution of sequence lengths, percent of calls that hit the KV prefix cache, and the batch size distribution over time. Notice the spike at 11:00 where batching dropped because of a small burst of low-latency requests.
[04:05] Liam O'Donnell: That cache hit % — what counts as a hit? Exact prefix?
[04:12] Priya Nair: It's a prefix heuristic — if the token prefix matches and we can reuse KV state, it's a hit. There are configurable TTLs and we show effective hit rate. In practice we've seen 20–45% reduction in tokens for document workflows.
[04:37] Rashida Khan: If we go private or VPC, does the console still show this telemetry?
[04:43] Alex Chen: Yes, the private control plane pushes metrics back securely; you can choose what telemetry to forward. For sensitive customers we support a minimized telemetry mode that still provides cost attribution metrics without payloads.

[05:05] Priya Nair: Now cost decomposition view — two-pane chart. On the left is total spend by route, on the right is breakdown for the selected route. For doc-summarize you can toggle model variants — quantized Llama-3-q4 vs a full fp16. The console simulates estimated cost delta if you switch models.
[05:34] Evan Wu: Is that simulation accurate? We need something we can put in a forecast.
[05:40] Priya Nair: It uses your historical token distribution and per-kernel cost profile. It's an estimate, not a guarantee, but close enough for forecasting and tradeoff discussions. We'll provide benchmark runs for your exact prompt set to tighten those numbers.

[06:10] [background noise]
[06:20] Maya Torres: Walk us through a playbook — how would Redwood recommend we reduce cost for the search-embedding route?
[06:29] Alex Chen: Sure — we start with three levers: 1) model choice, e.g., smaller embedding model for lower-sensitivity queries; 2) caching and dedupe on the embedding vectors; 3) batching and async processing. Priya will show a sample playbook in the console.
[06:47] Priya Nair: Playbook card — it lists observed problems (high per-call tokens, high latency), recommended changes, estimated savings, and a rollout plan: canary -> 50% -> full. You can pin the plan to a route and the console will simulate rollout impact.
[07:10] Liam O'Donnell: For canary, how do we route traffic? Does Redwood handle the split or do we control it?
[07:17] Priya Nair: Redwood supports route-level canary routing controlled by policy. You can route by percent, by header, or by region. Policies are stored in config and can trigger automatic rollback if performance or quality regressions are detected.
[07:34] Rashida Khan: Quality regressions — how is that measured? We need to ensure embeddings don't degrade search relevance.
[07:42] Priya Nair: You can attach a prompt set / eval to a route. The console will run evals after rollout steps and surface regression alerts in the Insights tab.

[08:05] Evan Wu: Let's talk numbers — for chat-widget, our traffic is high volume but short conversations. How would you price/attribute that vs a long-form doc-summarize?
[08:18] Alex Chen: The console shows cost per 1k tokens and cost per request. Chat-widget is often higher in requests but lower tokens/request, doc-summarize is the reverse. We give per-route unit economics so you can charge product teams on either tokens or per-call.
[08:37] Priya Nair: Also show the amortized GPU minute cost — for small messages that aren't batched, the per-call overhead is higher. If you can introduce a short delay to batch 50–100ms you may reduce cost by 15–30% depending on traffic shape.

[09:05] [short crosstalk]
[09:12] Maya Torres: That delay is acceptable for some features but not for our support-bot. We need latency SLOs there.
[09:19] Priya Nair: Right — in the console you can set latency SLOs per-route and the autoscaler respects that. We show expected cost impact when you tighten the SLO.

[09:40] Priya Nair: Quick demo of a rule: for support-bot we keep a small pool of fast GPUs and set batch max size low; for bulk-summarize we use larger batches and cheaper quantized instances.
[09:57] Liam O'Donnell: When you say cheaper instances, do you mean dedicated reserved capacity or lower-tier hardware?
[10:03] Priya Nair: Both. The routing layer can prefer cheaper model variants or route to dedicated capacity with reserved instances to achieve lower per-token cost. You can also route to on-prem GPU pools if you have them.

[10:20] Rashida Khan: For Private deploy, we have an air-gapped site. How much manual setup is needed to keep metrics flowing?
[10:29] Alex Chen: The private package includes a telemetry bridge; for air-gapped we provide an offline bundle and a small telemetry agent that you can push metrics from on-prem to your S3 or secure endpoint. We'll document the steps and provide runbooks.

[10:50] Priya Nair: Back to console — here's an anomaly view. It surfaces spikes in unit cost and links to sample requests. On a spike you can click to see the request payload (redacted by default) and the model variant used.
[11:15] Evan Wu: Are request payloads retained? We have retention constraints in EU.
[11:20] Alex Chen: Retention is configurable per-organization and per-route. For EU data residence we have region controls and can disable payload retention, only keeping metadata.

[11:40] Priya Nair: Now switching to the cost-sim tab where you can run "what-if" scenarios. For doc-summarize I toggle to q4 quantized model and the console shows estimated 28% cost savings and a median latency increase of 60ms. You can change the traffic mix slider to reflect your forecast.
[12:10] Maya Torres: Can we lock model versions per route to avoid accidental rollouts?
[12:16] Alex Chen: Yes — pin model versions and apply approval gates. We also have role-based access control so only certain users can change routing.

[12:34] Liam O'Donnell: Security — show me where SOC2 and SAML details live.
[12:38] Alex Chen: Under the Security tab we have compliance artifacts, audit logs, and the SSO config. For SAML you can paste IdP metadata and configure attribute mapping. For KMS we support customer-managed keys; you can see envelope encryption settings. We'll send the SOC2 pack in the follow-up.

[13:05] Priya Nair: We're going to run a short benchmark for you — Priya: can we grab a sample prompt set from Maya?
[13:12] Maya Torres: Yes we'll share a small set of typical user queries and a few long-doc summaries.
[13:18] Priya Nair: Great — we'll run bench on q4 quantized and fp16, measure p50/p95 latency and per-token cost, and feed the numbers into the console forecast.

[13:34] Evan Wu: On the billing side, is there a feature for predicted monthly spend per-product? I want a dashboard for finance.
[13:43] Alex Chen: There's a 'Cost Forecast' panel. It can project monthly spend based on seasonality and current traffic, and you can allocate by route to product owners. We also support tags for chargeback.

[14:05] Priya Nair: Ok quick demo of alerts and automation — you can set an action: if per-route cost increases by >20% over baseline, send Slack alert and spin up additional cheaper capacity or switch model variant.
[14:25] Rashida Khan: Does anyone support automatic rollback on quality regression?
[14:30] Priya Nair: Yes the rollout policy can include regression thresholds based on eval metrics and automatically rollback the change.

[15:00] [brief pause] Priya Nair: I want to call out a couple caveats — cached hits depend heavily on prompt stability; if your inputs vary widely you won't see high hit rates. Also batching gains depend on request shape and whether the client can tolerate micro-delay.
[15:22] Liam O'Donnell: Understood. On migration, what's the usual lift to get from current in-house inference to Redwood managed?
[15:30] Alex Chen: Typical lift: 2–6 weeks for a pilot. We usually onboard one or two routes, run benchmarks, then add more. If you want private deployment it adds 1–2 more weeks for network & KMS setup.
[15:48] Maya Torres: Is there an on-prem option that keeps everything inside our network? We have strict compliance with partner data.
[15:55] Alex Chen: Yes Private with local control plane or on-prem package. We can air-gap logs and only expose aggregated metrics if required.

[16:10] Evan Wu: Pricing model questions — reserved capacity vs usage: how do we decide?
[16:18] Priya Nair: If you have predictable steady throughput, reserved gives better unit economics. If spiky, a hybrid with burst on hosted is common. The console can simulate cost for both approaches using your traffic history.

[16:40] [noise: someone typing]
[16:50] Priya Nair: Let's go through the sample per-route cost export. I click export, we get a CSV showing route, model, tokens, gpu-minutes, and computed spend. We also demonstrate an allocation view that maps spend to teams.
[17:12] Evan Wu: Will that include per-invocation IDs so we can trace back to product events?
[17:18] Priya Nair: It can include request ids and minimal metadata (user-id hash) for traceability if you enable it.

[17:40] Alex Chen: Quick objection handling — some teams worry that console estimates are optimistic. We recommend you run our bench harness and use those numbers; we will include that in the follow-up. Anything else we should cover?
[17:55] Maya Torres: Can you show a quick example of how a product owner would check their route spend?
[18:02] Priya Nair: Sure — product owner logs in, home shows 'Your routes' card, they click into search-embedding and get a metric strip: spend this month, tokens, avg latency, and suggested optimizations. They can request a plan and assign it to SRE for rollout.

[18:26] Liam O'Donnell: About RBAC — can we restrict route visibility to only certain teams?
[18:32] Alex Chen: Yes roles and teams. We have org admin, billing-only, SRE, product, etc.

[18:45] [quiet for a bit]
[19:00] Priya Nair: Wrapping up, here's the concrete proposal: run a 2-week pilot for three routes (chat-widget, doc-summarize, search-embedding). We'll run benchmarks, provide forecasted cost deltas for quantization and batching, and deliver a route-level cost playbook.
[19:22] Maya Torres: That sounds good. Timeline?
[19:26] Alex Chen: Start next week. Deliverables: pricing spreadsheet incl. projected savings, benchmark results, SOC2 pack, and a security call.
[19:36] Rashida Khan: We'll share team contacts and traffic breakdown. Expect an email with sample data and SSO admin contact.

[19:50] Evan Wu: Any competitor notes? We looked at Anthropic and a few self-host options; your console automation and route mapping is compelling.
[19:59] Alex Chen: Appreciate that. We'll include a competitor comparison in the follow-up.

[20:10] Priya Nair: Last thing — quick note on quantization: not all models maintain parity on quality. We'll measure on your eval set and recommend which routes are safe.
[20:22] Liam O'Donnell: Cool.

[20:28] Alex Chen: Ok next steps recap — Alex will send pricing + SOC2 pack, Priya will run benchmarks, team will share sample prompts and traffic. I'll follow up with a calendar invite for the security deep dive.
[20:44] Maya Torres: Thanks folks, helpful demo.
[20:47] Liam O'Donnell: Thanks.
[20:49] Rashida Khan: Thanks everyone.

[20:55] [meeting ends]

Notes on transcription: Some words may be mis-transcribed (e.g., "KV" as "kay-vee" or "quant" as "quaint"). There was light background typing during the demo.
additional_notes: Shared artifacts mentioned: pricing spreadsheet (link to be emailed), SOC2 pack, sample bench harness. Customer requested per-route export to integrate with financial systems. Agreed pilot scope: 3 routes, 2 weeks.
